author: Jarrod Castillo
title: Astros ace fails to acclimate to American life following boisterous Shohei Ohtani claim - NewsBreak
text:
By Jarrod Castillo ,
1 hours ago Tatsuya Imai's claim before the start of the MLB season is aging like milk during a hot Texas summer day.
An ace in Japan, Imai was one of the more sought-after free agent pitchers during the offseason, with the Houston Astros eventually outbidding the rest of MLB for his services. Imai signed a three-year, $54 million contract with the Astros , with opt-outs after every year.
What's more, the Japanese ace's decision seemed to be rooted in an immense sense of confidence in himself , which is always needed to become a professional. However, it appears his decision to join the Astros has left much to be desired, especially after his tumultuous start to the 2026 season.
• Cleveland Browns coach flabbergasted by Shedeur Sanders question during NFL Draft
• Donald Trump halts state dinner speech to awkwardly praise Rory McIlroy and make request
Before the season, Imai let it be known that he wanted to join a team with no Japanese players, explaining that his desire stemmed from the excitement of being in a new place and from the challenge of establishing himself in the league and in the United States as a whole.
"Since they went to the US before me, I can ask them questions like 'What did you do in this situation?' right? But actually…I don’t really desire that. I want to have a sense of 'survival' on my own," he said to former MLB ace and Japanese legend Daisuke Matsuzaka.
"There are going to be cultural differences, but part of what excites me is how I’m going to figure out a way to get over these hurdles on my own."
What's more, the 27-year-old also stated that he would like an opportunity to face Shohei Ohtani, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and Roki Sasaki, which is why he opted to sign with a team without Japanese players.
"I want to take them down. I may as well," he said to Matsuzaka. "Of course, it looks fun to play alongside Ohtani, Yamamoto, and Sasaki. But I think being able to beat a team like that would be one of the most worthy things in my life."
As for who he wanted to face the most, he stated it was Ohtani, adding, "He would be the greatest test for me to see how good my fastball actually is."
That said, Imai has struggled mightily in MLB, posting a 7.27 ERA in three starts for the Astros. He was sidelined with right arm fatigue and subsequently sent down for rehab purposes.
While he was doing so, Imai's interpreter revealed that the star had not adjusted well to American life. “He’s not able to adjust to the American lifestyle,” Shio Enomoto said, according to The Athletic . “Baseball and outside of baseball. That’s probably the reason (for his arm fatigue).”

• Shohei Ohtani's classy off-camera gesture to young Dodgers fan
Enomoto added, “He thought it would be the same as in Japan, for example, eating dinner at the hotel. He thinks, even though he’s on the IL right now, he thinks it’s a positive thing to try and adjust and try to become better.”
In a recent rehab start in Double-A, he allowed five runs on six hits in two innings of work, showing just how much work he needs before getting back into MLB-level fitness.
For now, it remains to be seen how Imai will bounce back from what has been a rough start to his MLB career without the support of his countrymen to aid him through the trials and tribulations.
The good news is that there are still many months of baseball left. The bad news? If he's unable to turn things around, his claim before ever pitching in MLB could look even worse than it already is.
